messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Vectorizing to accept matrices
parts:
I think I figured out how to do it. More to come as I implement it.

The only issue is that we will break backward compatibility in certain cases, but at least it will be more consistent. We currently allow interchanging of row and column vectors, but once we allow matrices, I think we shouldn't allow it.

This is going to take some effort which includes rewriting a lot of our meta-template programs.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Vectorizing to accept matrices
parts:
Let's talk about this at the meeting.

I thought everyone was keen to allow
mixing of vectors, row vectors and arrays
as long as they were the same size.

I also think it would be an extreme amount of
backward compatibility to break at this point.

Were you thinking of replicating rows or
columns to make matrices? I think we also discussed
this and everyone thought it was too complex.
I sort of like the idea because it has a clean definition,
but agree that using it would probably be very confusing.

To deal with matrices, can't we just extend
vector views to wrap matrices and return the
elements in order? And the consistency checks.
What else is there? You can even use the () access
for matrices and perhaps put the three cases
together in the vector views (vector, row vector, and matrix).

- Bob

> mixing of vectors, row vectors and arrays

By doing this there is some ambiguity. I think we can still support that behavior, but then our language allows for ambiguity. Suppose y is a m by n matrix, mu is a vector of length m and sigma is a row vector of length n. If these are the arguments into normal_log() I imagine we want to evaluate it m x n times. Suppose m and n are the same. Then it's still clear that we should evaluate it m x m times, but it becomes ambiguous when y is a scalar. Should it be evaluated m x m times or just m times? If n and m are different, it should evaluate m x n times, right? I guess currently, it would not execute.

I agree that it's more flexible and I like the
type distintions. But it's flexing in a different
direction (replicating vectors up to matrices instead
of overloading vectors/row-vectors/arrays by size).
> I don't think it'll be that complex at all. We can talk a bit tomorrow in person.

I don't think it'd be complex to build, or to doc.
I just think it'd be confusing for users. And that's
the conclusion we came to when we went through this
the first time.

I realized the ramifications, so I am OK going without
replicating vectors in matrices and what not.

>> elements in order? And the consistency checks.
>> What else is there? You can even use the () access
>> for matrices and perhaps put the three cases
>> together in the vector views (vector, row vector, and matrix).

I think for the everything-matches-dimensions case it's
pretty easy to extend what we have.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Vectorizing to accept matrices
parts:
On 3/11/13 4:06 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> I wouldn't mind some automatic output being generated whenever this feature is accessed so that, for example, it says
> "Line 4: vector(n) theta expended to matrix(m,n)" or something like that.

We could do that. It makes sense as a warning.

The overall concern is that we can't be too aggressive with
warnings, or we'll get to the point where users just ignore
them all (i.e., not too high a false positive rate!).

- Bob

Yah, I was thinking about that. I wouldn't even exactly call it a "warning," as it's a feature we well might use intentionally. Perhaps a better (if more effortful) solution would be to have the program produce an annotated model, where the annotation would indicate vectorization, expansion of scalars/vectors/arrays, and any other tricks that might not be obvious from the code. Then there could be an option in the function call to print out or to access the annotated model.

parts:
I really like the idea of dumping out an annotated
program. I've never seen it done before, but it
seems like it'd be a good idea for just about any
programming language.

Maybe it'd be kind of like "show plan" in database
programming -- it would give you a notion of how
the code would play out in practice.

That's the computer science definition of "warning" --
not something illegal, but something that's flagged
because maybe you did it by mistake. For instance,
we get tons of warnings in Stan models for unused variables
because our code generation isn't as concise as it
could be (usually when you declare a variable and don't use
it, it's a mistake).

One warning I want to work on is declaring a parameter
and then not using it anywhere. That's usually
a mistake, but not always, because

parameters {
real<lower=0,upper=1> u;
}
model {}

is a perfectly reasonable uniform(0,1) sampler; but
usually an unused parameter is a mistake. We could
flag parameters that didn't show up on the left of
a twiddle (~), and/or ones that weren't used at all.

- Bob

vector(n) d, e;
etc.

On 3/11/13 8:19 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Another reason it can work to declare a parameter and not use it is if you're playing around with a model, adding and removing parameters to see what happens. In that case it can be convenient to alter the model without going back and cleaning up all the derivations.
>
> Which reminds me: it would be great to allow something like:
> real a, b, c;
> vector(n) d, e;

I have mixed feelings about this, but it's on the
near-term to-do list.

I find it makes it hard to scan for variables and to
doc what they're for. It's usually discouraged in programming
language style guides.

I can add it and then just soft-legislate against it in
our style guide, which nobody reads or believes in or
follows, but it'll make me feel better.

What I really do want, though is to

(a) allow declarations mixed in, rather than just
occurring at the top of a block, and

(b) allow compound declaration/definitions, like

real sum <- 0;

The motivation for (a) is that it's best to declare
variables near where they're defined, and (b) just
takes this to the logical endpoint of doing both at
the same time. This is good practice because it
lets you see the type quickly and easily see what
the defined value is, thus avoiding undefined variables.

- Bob
